lessons.title: Lesson 1: Checking your real screen time
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Find your daily screen time and top apps on your own phone.
This lesson builds toward: Using your own phone's settings, you will find your daily screen time, top apps and pickups or notifications, and compare them with your goals, writing down all three numbers.
Most people guess their screen time low. Your phone already tracks it. On an iPhone, open Settings and look for Screen Time. On many Android phones, open Settings and look for Digital Wellbeing. Names can differ by phone; if you can't find it, search Settings for "screen time".
Look at three numbers: your daily average, your top apps, and how many times you pick up your phone or get notifications. Pickups and notifications show how often your phone pulls you back.
There is no single perfect number. What matters is whether your screen time fits your goals: enough sleep, schoolwork or job done, time for friends in person, sports, rest and hobbies. Your numbers are a starting point, not a grade.
Step by step:
- Open Settings on your phone.
- Find Screen Time (iPhone) or Digital Wellbeing (many Android phones), or search Settings for "screen time".
- Write down your daily average, your top three apps and your pickups or notifications.
- Ask: does this fit my goals?
Words to know:
- Screen time: the amount of time you spend looking at a screen.
- Pickup: each time you pick up or unlock your phone.
- Digital wellbeing: using technology in a way that supports your health, goals and mood.
Try it now: Open your phone's screen time page. Write down your daily average, your top three apps and your daily pickups or notifications. Then write one goal screens are getting in the way of, if any.
You can now find your real screen time, top apps and pickups on your own phone.

check.q: What does your phone's "pickups" number show?
options: How often your phone pulls you back
check.why: Pickups and notifications show how often your phone pulls you back.

check.q: You cannot find Screen Time or Digital Wellbeing on your phone. What do you do?
options: Download a random app from a pop-up ad
check.why: Names differ by phone, so search Settings for "screen time".

lessons.title: Lesson 2: How apps keep you scrolling
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Spot the design features that pull you back in.
This lesson builds toward: In an app you use often, you will identify the design hooks that pull you back in and turn off or work around one, naming at least three hooks.
Many apps make money from your attention: the longer you stay, the more ads they show. So they are built to be hard to put down. Knowing the tricks makes it easier to choose for yourself.
Common hooks: endless scroll (there is never a bottom), autoplay (the next video starts on its own), notifications and red badges (they make you check), streaks (fear of losing them), likes and view counts (you keep checking for more), and "for you" feeds that learn exactly what keeps you watching.
None of this means you are weak. These features are designed by teams of experts. The answer is to add your own stopping points: turn off autoplay, set time limits, and decide before you open an app what you came to do.
Step by step:
- Open your top app from Lesson 1.
- Find each hook: endless scroll, autoplay, notifications, streaks, likes.
- Pick one hook to turn off or work around.
- Before opening an app, say what you came to do.
Words to know:
- Endless scroll: a feed that keeps loading more so there is no natural stopping point.
- Autoplay: when the next video starts by itself.
- Algorithm: the computer rules an app uses to choose what to show you next.
Try it now: Open your most-used app and list every hook you can find. Turn off one (for example autoplay or one type of notification) if the app lets you. Write which one you changed.
You can now spot the features apps use to keep you scrolling and add your own stopping points.

options: The next video starting on its own
check.why: Autoplay starts the next video without you choosing, which makes it hard to stop.

check.q: You open an app to reply to one message and end up scrolling for an hour. What habit helps next time?
options: Decide what you came to do before opening the app
check.why: Deciding what you came to do adds your own stopping point.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Screens, sleep and your mood
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set a screens-off time and a phone parking spot for the night.
This lesson builds toward: For your nights, you will set a screens-off time, a phone parking spot away from your bed and a sleep mode, with screens away about 30 minutes before your bedtime.
Sleep is when your body and brain recover. The CDC says teens 13 to 17 need 8 to 10 hours a night, and adults 18 and up need 7 or more. Late-night scrolling, gaming and messages are some of the biggest sleep thieves: you stay up later and wake up to notifications.
The CDC's sleep tips include keeping a regular bedtime and wake time, keeping your bedroom dark, calm and cool, and putting screens away about 30 minutes before bed. A phone parking spot outside your bed, or across the room, makes this easier. Use a cheap alarm clock if your phone is your alarm.
Notice how screens affect your mood too. If certain apps leave you anxious, angry or feeling worse about yourself, that is useful information. If you often feel low, can't sleep or feel hopeless, talk to a trusted adult or doctor. In the US you can call or text 988 any time; outside the US, call your local crisis line or emergency number.
Step by step:
- Choose your bedtime and count back 30 minutes: that is screens-off time.
- Pick a phone parking spot away from your bed.
- Turn on your phone's sleep or do not disturb mode for the night.
- Notice which apps change your mood, and how.
Words to know:
- Do not disturb: a phone setting that silences calls and notifications for a set time.
- Sleep schedule: going to bed and waking up at about the same time each day.
Official sources:
- CDC: About Sleep
- 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline
Try it now: Set your screens-off time and phone parking spot for tonight. Turn on sleep or do not disturb mode. Tomorrow, write how you slept and how you felt in the morning.
You can now protect your sleep with a screens-off time, a phone parking spot and do not disturb mode.

check.q: What is a phone parking spot?
options: A place away from your bed where the phone stays at night
check.why: Parking the phone away from your bed makes late-night scrolling harder.

check.q: Your bedtime is 10:30 pm. When do you put screens away?
check.why: Putting screens away about 30 minutes before bed helps you sleep.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Taming notifications and setting app limits
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn off non-essential notifications and set a limit on one app.
This lesson builds toward: Using your phone's settings, you will turn off non-essential notifications and set a daily limit on your top app, turning off at least three apps' notifications.
Every notification is an interruption. It can take a while to get your focus back after checking your phone, which slows down homework, practice, studying or work. You decide which apps get to interrupt you.
Keep notifications for people and things that matter (calls and messages from family, school or work alerts, your ride). Turn them off for games, shopping and most social media. You can usually do this in Settings, under Notifications, app by app.
Both iPhone and Android let you set daily time limits on apps, and focus or do not disturb modes for school, work or practice. When you hit a limit, the phone reminds you. You can override it, but the pause gives you a choice. Some people also move tempting apps off the home screen or log out after use, so opening them takes a little more effort.
Step by step:
- Open Settings, then Notifications.
- Keep people and important alerts; turn off games, shopping and most social media.
- Set a daily limit on your top app (Screen Time or Digital Wellbeing).
- Turn on a focus or do not disturb mode during school, work or practice.
- Move one tempting app off your home screen.
Words to know:
- Notification: a message or alert that pops up on your phone from an app.
- App limit: a daily time limit you set for an app.
- Focus mode: a setting that silences distractions while you work, study or rest.
Try it now: Go through your notifications and turn off at least three apps that don't need to interrupt you. Then set a daily time limit on your top app from Lesson 1.
You can now control which apps can interrupt you, set app limits and use focus modes.

check.q: Why can notifications slow down your homework?
options: Each one interrupts you, and it takes time to get your focus back
check.why: Every notification is an interruption that pulls your focus away.

check.q: A shopping app sends you sale alerts all day. What do you do?
options: Keep them; you might miss a deal
Turn off that app's notifications in Settings
Turn off your calls and messages instead
check.why: Keep notifications for people and important alerts; turn off shopping and games.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: A healthier feed and less comparison
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Change your feed so it leaves you feeling better, not worse.
This lesson builds toward: On your main social app, you will change your feed by muting or unfollowing accounts that make you feel worse and following ones that help you grow, changing at least two accounts each way.
Social media shows highlight reels: the best photos, filters and edits. Comparing your everyday life to someone else's best moments can leave you feeling you are not enough. Remember what you see is chosen and edited.
You can train your feed. Unfollow or mute accounts that make you feel bad about your body, money or life. Follow people who teach you something, make you laugh or support your goals: your sport, music, art, a career you want, your culture. Use "not interested" options when the app offers them. The algorithm learns from what you watch, so watch on purpose.
Check in with yourself: "How do I feel after 10 minutes on this app?" If the answer is often worse, change what you follow or how long you stay. If someone online is being cruel to you, tell a trusted adult; the Koach Learn course Staying Safe from Cyberbullying shows you what to do.
Step by step:
- Scroll your feed for two minutes and notice how each account makes you feel.
- Unfollow or mute two accounts that make you feel worse.
- Follow two accounts that teach, inspire or make you laugh.
- Use "not interested" on content you don't want.
Words to know:
- Highlight reel: only the best moments, chosen and edited to look good.
- Mute: hide someone's posts without unfollowing or telling them.
Try it now: Spend two minutes on your main app and rate how each of the first ten posts makes you feel (better, same, worse). Mute or unfollow two "worse" accounts and follow two that help you grow.
You can now shape your feed so it supports your mood and goals instead of making you compare.

check.q: What does the app's algorithm learn from?
options: What you watch and do in the app
check.why: The algorithm learns from what you watch, so watching on purpose shapes your feed.

check.q: You feel worse after 10 minutes on an app most days. What do you try?
options: Follow more accounts like the ones that upset you
Change who you follow or how long you stay
check.why: If an app often leaves you feeling worse, change your feed or your time on it.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Making and testing your screen plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a screen plan and test it for seven days.
This lesson builds toward: Using what you set up in this course, you will write a personal screen plan, follow it for seven days and compare your results with your starting numbers, with every part of the plan and a before-and-after comparison.
A plan turns good ideas into habits. Your screen plan is short and specific, and it is yours: you choose the goals.
Include: your daily screen time goal, your top two apps to limit (with limits set in your phone), your notification changes, your screens-off time and phone parking spot, two things to do instead of scrolling when you are bored (walk, practice your sport, draw, call a friend, read, cook), and one feed change.
Test it for seven days, then compare your screen time, pickups and sleep with your numbers from Lesson 1. Keep what worked and change what didn't. Slipping up one day is normal; just start again the next day. Telling a friend or family member about your plan, or doing it together, makes it easier.
Step by step:
- Write your screen time goal.
- Set limits on your top two apps.
- List your notification changes and screens-off time.
- Write two things to do instead of scrolling.
- Test for seven days and compare with Lesson 1.
Words to know:
- Screen plan: your own written rules for when, where and how much you use screens.
Try it now: Final task: write your screen plan with all the parts, set the limits in your phone, and follow it for seven days. On day seven, compare your screen time, pickups and sleep with your numbers from Lesson 1.
You can now make, follow and adjust a personal screen plan that protects your sleep, focus and mood.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Goal and app limits No screen time goal, or limits not set in the phone. A daily screen time goal and limits set on the top two apps. Also uses a focus mode for school, work or practice. Notifications No notification changes. At least three non-essential apps' notifications turned off, keeping people and important alerts. Also moved a tempting app off the home screen. Sleep plan No screens-off time or phone parking spot. A screens-off time about 30 minutes before bed and a parking spot away from the bed. Sleep or do not disturb mode is on every night of the test. Feed and alternatives No feed change, or no alternatives to scrolling. One feed change and two things to do instead of scrolling. Notes how the feed change affected their mood. Seven-day test The plan was not tested, or results were not compared. Followed for seven days, with screen time, pickups and sleep compared with Lesson 1. Says what to keep and what to change for next week. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What do you compare at the end of your seven-day test?
options: Your screen time, pickups and sleep with your Lesson 1 numbers
check.why: Comparing with your starting numbers shows what worked.

check.q: You get bored and reach for your phone. What does your plan say to do?
options: Do one of your two things instead of scrolling, like a walk or a call
check.why: Your plan lists two things to do instead of scrolling when you are bored.
